سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية ابيي حكومة السودان , حكومة كامل ادريس , دول الجوار , كردفان 0 الخارجية السودانية الخرطوم، 23 أبريل 2026 – قالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية إن القوات المسلحة ليس لديها أي صلة بحادثة قصف سوق النعام بمنطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها بين السودان ودولة جنوب السودان. ووصف بيان للخارجية ليل أمس الحادثة بالمؤسفة، مشيراً إلى أن الحادثة تشبه الجرائم التي ما زالت ترتكبها قوات الدعم السريع، مثلما حدث في ديسمبر 2025 بكادوقلي عاصمة ولاية جنوب كردفان، حينما استهدفت معسكر قوات الأمم المتحدة المؤقتة لأبيي «يونسفا»، مما أدى وقتها إلى مقتل عدد من قوات حفظ السلام من الكتيبة البنغلاديشية، فضلاً عن استهداف قوافل المساعدات الإنسانية. وأسفر الهجوم وقتها عن إخلاء قوات «يونيسفا» لمعسكرها في كادوقلي، بينما لم يتبنَّ أيٌّ من طرفي القتال عملية القصف. وأضاف بيان الخارجية أن حكومة السودان تعرب عن أسفها البالغ لسقوط ضحايا مدنيين «فيما زُعم أنها ضربة بمسيّرة في سوق النعام بمنطقة أبيي». وجدد البيان التضامن مع أسر الضحايا والأمنيات للجرحى بعاجل الشفاء. وتعرض سوق النعام المعروف في جنوب السودان بسوق أمييت لقصف بمسيّرة استراتيجية أسفر عن قتلى وجرحى واشتعال حرائق واسعة. وأعلنت الأمم المتحدة أمس مقتل 80 شخصاً على الأقل في هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت منطقة أبيي، فيما عالج أفرادها 27 مصاباً، مؤكدة استمرار التحقق من أعداد الضحايا وبقاء أشخاص آخرين في عداد المفقودين. واتهمت حكومة جنوب السودان الجيش السوداني بقصف سوق النعام في بلدة أبيي المتنازع عليها، واستدعت وزارة الخارجية هناك السفير السوداني ونقلت إليه احتجاجها على القصف، فيما لم تعلق الخرطوم على الحادثة. الكلمات: سوق النعام، أبيي، وزارة الخارجية السودانية، جنوب السودان، قصف بمسيّرة، الأمم المتحدة، يونيسفا، كادوقلي، الجيش السوداني، الدعم السريع مقالات ذات صلة احباط هجوم للدعم السريع في المحور الشرقي حراك دبلوماسي محموم بين عدة عواصم لإقرار هدنة إنسانية في السودان السودان: النيابة العامة تُشكل لجنة للتحقيق في مقتل ناشط تحت التعذيب السودان يزحف لإحتلال المرتبة الثانية Adel Abdelrheem 23 أكتوبر 2026 • تحديث : 23 أكتوبر 2026 الأرشيف SUDAN الخرطوم/ عادل عبد الرحيم/ الأناضول نفت الحكومة السودانية، الجمعة، صلة الجيش بهجوم بطائرة مسيرة استهدف سوق النعام في منطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها مع جنوب السودان، وأسفر عن مقتل 153 شخصا، بحسب حصيلة أعلنتها السلطات المحلية. والأربعاء، أعلن وزير الإعلام المكلف في إدارة منطقة أبيي التابعة لجنوب السودان، يوحنا أكول نقور، ارتفاع حصيلة قتلى هجوم بمسيرة استهدف سوق أميت، المعروف محليا بسوق النعام، إلى 153 شخصا، مقارنة بحصيلة سابقة بلغت 73 قتيلا. وقالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية، في بيان، إنه "لا توجد أي صلة للقوات المسلحة السودانية بهذه الحادثة المؤسفة"، معربة عن بالغ أسف الحكومة لسقوط ضحايا مدنيين في الهجوم. وأضافت أن الحكومة السودانية تجدد تضامنها مع أسر الضحايا، وتمنياتها للجرحى بالشفاء العاجل. واعتبرت الوزارة أن الحادثة "تشبه الجرائم التي ما زالت المليشيا الإرهابية تستمر في ارتكابها"، في إشارة إلى قوات الدعم السريع. ولفتت إلى هجوم استهدف مقر قوة الأمم المتحدة الأمنية المؤقتة لأبيي (يونيسفا) في مدينة كادوقلي جنوبي السودان، في 13 ديسمبر/ كانون الأول 2025، ما أدى إلى مقتل عدد من قوات حفظ السلام من الكتيبة البنغلاديشية آنذاك، فضلا عن استهداف قوافل مساعدات إنسانية. وفي اليوم ذاته، أعلن الجيش السوداني مقتل 6 أشخاص وإصابة 7 آخرين من أفراد بعثة الأمم المتحدة، في هجوم بثلاثة صواريخ أطلقتها مسيرة اتهم قوات الدعم السريع بتنفيذه ضد مقر البعثة في كادوقلي. في المقابل، نفت قوات الدعم السريع مسؤوليتها عن الهجوم. والاثنين، استدعت وزارة خارجية جنوب السودان السفير السوداني لدى جوبا، عصام كرار، احتجاجا على الهجوم الذي استهدف سوق أمييت في منطقة أبيي، وأسفر عن سقوط قتلى وجرحى من المدنيين. والخميس، أعلنت الأمم المتحدة مقتل 80 شخصا على الأقل وإصابة 27 آخرين في الهجوم، مشيرة إلى أنها لم تتمكن بعد من تحديد الجهة المسؤولة عنه. وتعد "أبيي" منطقة غنية بالنفط ومتنازعا عليها بين السودان وجنوب السودان، وحصلت على وضع إداري خاص بموجب اتفاقية السلام الشامل الموقعة في 9 يناير/ كانون الثاني 2005. وتعد المنطقة جسرا بين شمالي السودان وجنوبه، حيث تسكن في الشمال قبائل "المسيرية" العربية، أما جنوبا فتستوطن قبائل "الدينكا" الإفريقية. ويأتي الهجوم في ظل استمرار الحرب بالسودان بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع منذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023، على خلفية خلاف بشأن دمج الأخيرة في المؤسسة العسكرية. وأسفرت الحرب عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص، التي قد تتخذها للضغط على سلطات بورتسودان لوقف ذلك القصف الذي وصف بـ«الممنهج». وإلى ذلك، قال عثمان عبدالرحمن، الناطق الرسمي باسم القوى المدنية المتحدة «قِمم» في السودان، إن وتيرة القصف الجوي باستخدام الطائرات المسيّرة تصاعدت خلال الأسبوعين الماضيين، مستهدفةً أسواق: نيالا، والنعام على الحدود السودانية الجنوبية، والضعين، في هجمات قال إنها تتكرر يوميًا. واعتبر عبدالرحمن، في تصريحات لـ«العين الإخبارية»، أن استهداف مناطق لا تظهر فيها، مظاهر عسكرية يعكس تحولًا في نهج قيادة الجيش، الذي تحرك قراراته الحركة الإسلامية، ولا سيما سلاحي الطيران الحربي والمسير. وأوضح أن «قِمم» ترى أن هذه الهجمات تأتي بعد إخفاق الجيش في تحقيق انتصارات ميدانية، متهما الحركة الإسلامية بالسعي إلى تهجير المواطنين، وبث الرعب بينهم. استهداف الحواضن الاجتماعية وأشار إلى أن قيادة الجيش تتجه إلى تحويل الحرب من مواجهة عسكرية إلى استهداف للحواضن الاجتماعية، بما يهدد النسيج المجتمعي ويعرض المدنيين لمزيد من المخاطر. ودعا القوى المدنية والسياسية المؤمنة بالتغيير والتحول المدني الديمقراطي، داخل السودان وخارجه، إلى توحيد جهودها السياسية والإعلامية، وتوسيع نطاق التحرك لإيصال ما وصفه بالانتهاكات والجرائم إلى مؤسسات المجتمع الدولي، مشددًا على ضرورة التحرك لوقف الهجمات وحماية المدنيين. تحرك دولي ومحاسبة المسؤولين وفيما يتعلق بالمحاسبة، قال عبدالرحمن إن الانتهاكات التي تتحدث عنها «قِمم» موثقة، وإن الأولوية تتمثل في اتخاذ خطوات عاجلة لمحاسبة المسؤولين عنها. وأشار إلى أن الإدانات التي صدرت عن المبعوث الشخصي للأمين العام للأمم المتحدة، بيكا هافيستو، تعكس وصول المعلومات المتعلقة بالانتهاكات إلى المجتمع الدولي، مشيرًا إلى أن تشكيل لجنة لتقصي الحقائق يظل خيارًا ممكنًا في إطار الآليات والإجراءات الدولية. وحذّر من أن استمرار قصف الأسواق سيدفع «قِمم» إلى تكثيف تحركاتها الخارجية وتوسيع اتصالاتها الدولية، إلى جانب القنوات الرسمية التي تتحرك من خلالها. وأعرب عن اعتقاده بأن التحرك الدولي هذه المرة قد يتخذ منحى أكثر فاعلية، متوقعًا فرض عقوبات على قادة الجيش، ولم يستبعد وصول الضغوط، إلى إجراءات أشد بحق قيادته في بورتسودان، وعلى رأسها عبدالفتاح البرهان. حظر الطيران الحربي والمسير وعن المطالب العاجلة، شدد عبدالرحمن على ضرورة أن يصدر مجلس الأمن الدولي قرارًا بحظر تحليق الطيران الحربي والطائرات المسيّرة التابعة للجيش فوق الأراضي السودانية. كما دعا الولايات المتحدة إلى الضغط من أجل تمرير قرار بحظر السلاح يشمل جميع الأراضي السودانية، وحث أعضاء مجلس الأمن على دعم هذه الخطوة، معتبرًا أنها قد تسهم في وقف الهجمات وحماية المدنيين. واختتم بتأكيد ضرورة الانتقال من الإدانة الدولية إلى إجراءات عملية تضع حدًا للهجمات على الأسواق والمناطق المدنية، وتضمن محاسبة المسؤولين عن الانتهاكات. في السياق نفسه، حمل رئيس حركة تحرير السودان الديمقراطية حسب النبي محمود، في تصريحات لـ«العين الإخبارية»، عبدالفتاح البرهان وقيادة الجيش السوداني المسؤولية المباشرة عن «المجازر التي قال إنها تستهدف المدنيين في مناطق متفرقة من البلاد»، مشيرًا إلى سقوط أكثر من 316 مدنيًا خلال أسبوع واحد، في مناطق تمتد من كردفان والنيل الأزرق إلى دارفور. واتهم قيادة الجيش بتوجيه العمليات العسكرية ضد قبائل ومناطق بعينها، مستشهدًا بتصريحات قال إن رئيس أركان الجيش أدلى بها في الشهر الأول من الحرب، وتضمنت تحديد قبائل ومناطق جغرافية. وأضاف أن استهداف ما وصفه بـ«الحواضن الاجتماعية للتمرد» مستمر منذ اندلاع القتال، وأسفر عن مقتل آلاف المدنيين لمجرد انتمائهم إلى دارفور وكردفان. واعتبر رئيس حركة تحرير السودان الديمقراطية أن قيادة الجيش تتبنى نهجًا يهدد وحدة السودان، متهمًا إياها بالسعي إلى فصل دارفور وكردفان. وقال إن العمليات العسكرية في هذه المناطق تستخدم تقنيات متطورة، لإلحاق أكبر قدر من الضرر بالسكان والمناطق المستهدفة. تحقيق دولي في جرائم الحرب وطالب محمود بإجراء تحقيق دولي مستقل في الانتهاكات التي اتهم الجيش والجماعات المتحالفة معه بارتكابها، بما في ذلك جرائم حرب وإبادة جماعية، داعيًا إلى تشكيل فريق محايد يتمتع بالقدرة على التحقيق في الوقائع وتحديد المسؤوليات. وشدد على أن المساءلة ستظل مطلبًا للشعب السوداني وللمجتمعين الدولي والإقليمي، لافتًا إلى أن بعض الوقائع التي تحدث عنها جرت، أمام قوات دولية. وأشار إلى الهجوم الذي قال إنه استهدف سوق النعام، وأسفر عن مقتل أكثر من 100 شخص وإصابة العشرات، معتبرًا أن وقوعه في منطقة توجد فيها قوات أممية ولا تنتشر فيها قوات عسكرية سودانية يستدعي تحقيقًا مستقلًا لتحديد ملابسات الهجوم والمسؤولية عنه. آليات فعالة وجدد مطالبته بتشكيل لجنة مستقلة ذات صلاحيات واسعة للتحقيق في جرائم الحرب والانتهاكات التي نسبها إلى البرهان والقوى المتحالفة معه، داعيًا المجتمع الدولي إلى الاستماع إلى القوى الوطنية السودانية ودعم تحالف السودان التأسيسي. كما طالب بفرض حظر على الطيران في جميع أنحاء السودان، مستندًا إلى قرار سابق لمجلس الأمن بشأن حظر الطيران في دارفور. وأقر بأن القرار السابق لم يحقق الفاعلية المطلوبة، لكنه رأى أن توسيع نطاق الحظر ليشمل كامل الأراضي السودانية، ضمن المقترح الأمريكي الذي أشار إليه، قد يسهم في حماية المدنيين إذا اقترن بآليات رقابة دولية وقوات أممية للردع. وأكد أن أي تحرك دولي يستهدف حماية المدنيين ينبغي أن يترافق مع آليات فعالة لمراقبة تنفيذ القرارات، والتحقيق في الانتهاكات، ومحاسبة المسؤولين عنها. السودان غرفة الأخبار #حوارات_العين_الإخبارية #تقارير_خاصة السريع» الأخبار الجيش السوداني يكثف هجماته الجوية على مواقع «الدعم السريع» 22 أكتوبر 2026 في الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان , دارفور , كردفان 0 صورة نشرتها الإدارة المدنية التابعة لقوات الدعم السريع لسوق موقف الجنينة بنيالا - ارشيف الخرطوم 22 أكتوبر 2026 – واصل الجيش السوداني، الخميس، هجماته الجوية على مواقع وتجمعات قوات الدعم السريع في إقليمي دارفور وكردفان، مستهدفاً مناطق متفرقة في اقليمي دارفور وكردفان. ومنذ نحو أسبوعين ابتدر الجيش السوداني عملية جوية واسعة النطاق؛ حيث ظل يهاجم وبشكل شبه يومي مدناً خاضعة لسيطرة الدعم السريع في إقليمي دارفور وكردفان. وقال شهود عيان في مدينة الفاشر بولاية شمال دارفور لـ«سودان تربيون» إن “مسيّرات تابعة للجيش هاجمت مواقع الدعم السريع في قصر الضيافة – مقر الحكومة السابقة-، والسوق الكبير، ومجمع الوزارات وسط المدينة، إلى جانب تمركزات في حي الدرجة غربي الفاشر”. وأفاد الشهود بأن الهجمات أدت إلى تدمير عتاد حربي، علاوة على إحداث خسائر فادحة طالت ممتلكات المواطنين في سوق الفاشر الكبير، بجانب إحداث أضرار في مسجد السلطان علي دينار بوسط المدينة. وفي شرق دارفور، قال شهود إن الهجمات استهدفت منطقة أبو جابرة الغنية بالنفط؛ حيث طالت الغارات شاحنات محملة بالوقود أدت إلى احتراقها، بجانب مركبات عسكرية تابعة للدعم السريع وسيارات مدنية، وامتدت هجمات الطيران إلى مدينة بابنوسة بولاية غرب كردفان. وقال مصدر عسكري لـ«سودان تربيون» إن تكثيف الجيش هجماته في دارفور وكردفان يهدف إلى إضعاف القدرات الدفاعية والهجومية لقوات الدعم السريع، وتجريدها من الوسائل التي يمكن أن تشكل خطراً عسكرياً، تعقبها مرحلة الاكتساح البري لنظافة ما تبقى من كردفان ودارفور. وأكد أن الهجمات الأخيرة حققت أهدافها، وأسفرت عن مقتل العشرات من عناصر الدعم السريع وتدمير مخازن للوقود ومنظومات للدفاع الجوي في نيالا والفاشر. وأمس الأربعاء، تعرضت مدنا نيالا والضعين لهجمات عنيفة بالطيران المسيّر؛ حيث هاجمت مقرات للدعم السريع في الضعين، علاوة على منازل قيادات عسكرية ومخازن الذخيرة والوقود في مدينة نيالا التي تعرض مطارها لهجوم أيضاً. وكانت الدعم السريع وحلفاؤها في «تأسيس» اتهموا الجيش بقتل عشرات المدنيين جراء غارات جوية استهدفت مدن نيالا والضعين، والدبب وسوق النعام، إلى جانب مدن النهود والأضية وأبو زبد ود بندة خلال الأسبوع الجاري. الكلمات: الجيش السوداني الفاشر. حرب السودان دارفور غارات جوية قوات الدعم السريع كردفان نيالا مقالات ذات صلة تجاوز عدد الفارين الخارجية هناك السفير السوداني ونقلت إليه احتجاجها على القصف، فيما لم تعلق الخرطوم على الحادثة. ونقلت “رويترز” عن وزير الإعلام في حكومة تصريف الأعمال في أبيي الثلاثاء الماضي أن عدد الضحايا الذين سقطوا جراء تلك الهجمات تضاعف من 73 إلى 153 قتيلاً. وقال مكتب المتحدث باسم الأمين العام إن قوة الأمم المتحدة الأمنية المؤقتة لأبيي «يونيسفا» أخمدت الحرائق الكبيرة التي تسببت فيها الهجمات على سوق أميت وتوداتش، بينما يواصل أفراد حفظ السلام إجلاء الضحايا وتقديم المساعدة الطبية. ويجري أفراد دائرة الأمم المتحدة للأعمال المتعلقة بالألغام تقييماً للمناطق المتضررة للكشف عن أي ذخائر غير منفجرة. وأوضح المتحدث باسم الأمين العام، ستيفان دوجاريك، رداً على سؤال بشأن الجهة المسؤولة عن الهجوم، أن الأمم المتحدة ليست في وضع يسمح لها بتحديد المسؤولية رسمياً في هذه المرحلة. وتواصل «يونيسفا» اتصالاتها بحكومتي السودان وجنوب السودان والأطراف المعنية الأخرى، دعماً لجهود خفض التصعيد. وجددت الأمم المتحدة دعوة الأمين العام، الذي أدان الهجمات، إلى الحكومتين اتخاذ جميع الخطوات الممكنة لمنع هجمات أخرى والحفاظ على وضع أبيي المنزوع السلاح، مع مواصلة الحوار عبر الآليات القائمة، بما في ذلك الاجتماع المقبل للآلية السياسية والأمنية المشتركة المقرر عقده في الخرطوم. مساعي إنهاء الحرب وفي جنيف، تشارك الأمم المتحدة الحكومة السويسرية في استضافة الجولة السادسة من المشاورات بشأن السودان، بمشاركة أطراف دولية وإقليمية تسعى إلى تنسيق جهودها لإنهاء الحرب. وقال المبعوث الشخصي للأمين العام، بيكا هافيستو، خلال «الاجتماع التشاوري السادس لتعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام من أجل السودان»، إن اللقاء يتيح فرصة لتقييم الجهود الجماعية والنظر في سبل تعزيز التنسيق بين المبادرات المختلفة. وتهدف الجلسات إلى استكشاف سبل عملية للمضي قدماً، بما في ذلك مسار نحو مرحلة سياسية انتقالية تعكس تطلعات الشعب السوداني، مع التركيز على إرساء أسس حوار شامل وذي مصداقية يدعم عملية سياسية يقودها السودانيون. وأضاف هافيستو أن الاستماع إلى وجهات نظر دول المنطقة والنظر في كيفية منع المزيد من التدهور وامتداد تداعيات الأزمة أمران أساسيان. وأكد التزامه بعقد هذه الاجتماعات كل ثلاثة أشهر للحفاظ على الزخم والمساعدة في بلورة استجابات عملية للوضع المتغير. ورداً على سؤال عما إذا كانت الأمم المتحدة تعتزم عرض خطة موحدة على طرفي الحرب أو بدء عملية تفاوضية بعد اجتماع جنيف، أوضح دوجاريك أنه لم يقل إن الاجتماع سيفضي إلى خطة موحدة، وإن العمل في هذا الاتجاه مستمر. ودعا إلى انتظار اختتام الاجتماع، مشيراً إلى أنه، وفقاً لما لديه من معلومات محدودة، لا يتوقع إعلاناً متكاملاً على النحو الوارد في السؤال. وأكد أن هدف الاجتماع، كما أوضح هافيستو، هو استكشاف سبل عملية للتقدم نحو مرحلة سياسية انتقالية تضع تطلعات الشعب السوداني في صميمها، داعياً إلى متابعة المؤتمر الصحفي للمبعوث في جنيف، الذي قال إنه ربما كان لا يزال منعقداً أو اختتم قبل وقت قصير. ethiopia.content: Kenya launches emergency aid efforts as hundreds flee deadly clashes in Ethiopia For You News Faida Cafe Shows Radio TV Podcasts Live Events Search Kenya launches emergency aid efforts as hundreds flee deadly clashes in Ethiopia By Kenneth Gachie October 23, 2026 09:00 (EAT) Add as a Preferred Source on Google Follow us Follow on Whatsapp Follow on Google Follow on Twitter A file photo of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed . Audio By Vocalize The Kenya Red Cross Society has launched an emergency relief operation in Moyale, Marsabit County, to support families fleeing deadly clashes in neighbouring Ethiopia, with the initial response targeting 1,000 households in urgent need of assistance. In a statement on Thursday, the humanitarian organisation said the families had arrived in Kenya with few belongings and urgently needed shelter, food, safe water and healthcare as fighting continued across parts of southern Ethiopia. Red Cross teams are working with the Marsabit County Government, national authorities and partners to establish temporary shelters and distribute essential supplies, including tents, blankets, sleeping mats, jerrycans and kitchen sets. The organisation is also providing Super Cereal, a fortified porridge flour for young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers, as well as first aid to those requiring medical attention. In addition, the agency is helping family members who have been separated during the displacement reconnect through its family-links service. “Our priority is to make sure every family arriving in Moyale is safe, sheltered and treated with dignity. Our volunteers and staff are on the ground and will continue to respond as needs evolve,” said Secretary General Ahmed Idris. The families have fled fighting in Moyale, Ethiopia, where security forces from the Oromia and Somali regions clashed on Thursday amid rising tensions over a regional flag dispute. The violence erupted in Moyale on the Ethiopian side of the border following tensions over the display of the Somali Regional State flag at a local administrative office in an area administered by Ethiopia's Oromia Regional State. Oromia and the Somali Regional State are two of Ethiopia's federal regions, home predominantly to Oromo and ethnic Somali communities respectively. Both communities have longstanding ties to the border area. The killing of a 13-year-old girl on Oct. 18 further heightened tensions before armed confrontations rocked with heavy gunfire broke out Wednesday night and intensified Thursday. Residents reported heavy gunfire involving regional security forces, while local officials said the fighting had spread to Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero districts in southern Ethiopia, according to Ethiopian local media stations. Homes and trading centers were burned, disrupting commercial activities and forcing residents to abandon their properties. The exact number of people killed or injured remained unclear, with no independently verified casualty figures available. Moyale, approximately 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and about 770 kilometers (478 miles) south of Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, by road, is a major commercial crossing between the two countries. The border town serves communities in both countries, with close family and trading connections making it an important route for people fleeing insecurity. During the visit, Abiy said Ethiopia must move beyond meeting its immediate economic needs and invest in scientific and technological development that would benefit future generations. "Ethiopia's next chapter is about transforming its immense potential and abundant natural resources into tangible development, technological advancement, and shared prosperity," Abiy said in a social media post following the visit. The prime minister stressed that reliable and sustainable energy was essential to industrialisation, manufacturing, digital infrastructure and broader economic development. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn He said nuclear technology offered Ethiopia an opportunity to strengthen its energy security while supporting scientific progress across several sectors. Beyond electricity generation, Abiy highlighted the potential applications of nuclear technology in healthcare, agriculture, industry and environmental protection, describing these fields as important areas for innovation and sustainable development. The Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission is responsible for establishing the institutional and technical foundations of the country's national nuclear energy programme. Abiy emphasised the importance of developing skilled professionals, strengthening scientific research and transferring technical knowledge to future generations. During the visit, the prime minister also spoke about Ethiopia's broader development ambitions, saying the country had a responsibility to lay the foundations for the advancement of Ethiopian civilisation. He said national development should not be limited to addressing immediate needs but should also focus on creating a lasting legacy for future generations across all sectors. The prime minister underscored the importance of ensuring that nuclear energy development proceeds peacefully, safely, responsibly and sustainably. Ethiopia's government views nuclear technology as part of its long-term efforts to expand energy capacity, strengthen scientific institutions and support economic transformation. Furthermore, he added that significant investments are being carried out toward improving market systems and building a sustainable rural economy. He highlighted that indigenous knowledge of farmers and pastoralists has been integrated to implement climate-smart agricultural practices. Moving forward, he emphasized that collaboration among the government, regional states, researchers, and development partners is crucial to realizing the transformation of the food system. The World Food Program (WFP) Country Director for Ethiopia Zlatan Milišić for his part praised Ethiopia's effective achievements in leveraging its youth potential, natural resources, and indigenous knowledge to transform its food system. The national strategies and policies established by the government in the sector have laid a strong foundation for these efforts, he noted. ethiopia.title: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Fighting in Border Town Moyale Spreads to Three More Districts, Exchange of Heavy Gunfire 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — What started as a dispute over the raising of a Somali Regional State flag in Moyale town, Borana Zone, Oromia Region, followed by the killing of a 13-year-old girl on October 18, has escalated into sustained fighting, with security forces from the Oromia and Somali regions exchanging heavy gunfire. Tensions that had been building since Wednesday night erupted into open clashes on Thursday and spread to parts of Gumi Eldallo, Wachile, and Arero districts in South Oromia, residents and local security officials told Addis Standard . Moyale town residents told Addis Standard that fighting broke out at dawn on Thursday, around 5:30 a.m., in several locations, including Malab, Chamuk, Bole, Kebele 01, and Waqo Dogo localities. South Oromia security officials confirmed that the fighting later spread to parts of the East Borana Zone, including Melka Guba kebele in Gumi Eldallo District, Melka Adi and Melka Chophi kebeles in Wachile District, and an area known as Ela Orbi in Arero District. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn A resident of Moyale, Waqo Hussein, claims attempts by Somali Regional State special forces to raise a flag, along with the killing of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa and unverified rumors of assassination attempt against a city official on Tuesday evening as factors that contributed to the escalation. Regarding Thursday's fighting, Waqo said, "We took measures to defend and protect ourselves." A Moyale town official on the Oromia side also said that fighting broke out at dawn in several locations, claiming it as "a war declared on our people early in the morning by forces who have recently been making various provocations." A Somali resident of Moyale who fled with his family to the Ilu area of Moyale, Kenya, rejected the allegations from the Oromia side but confirmed that the flag dispute was central to the conflict. "This morning, October 22, it was forces from the Borana side who opened fire on us; they prevented us from raising our flag," he said. He further alleged that after the fighting began, forces from the Borana side burned houses belonging to Somali (Garre community) residents, along with offices and various signboards. Another Moyale resident from the Chamuk area told Addis Standard that government-backed Somali Regional forces equipped with heavy weaponry had attacked them. He said residents had identified the alleged attackers through identity cards recovered from deceased combatants and military communication equipment. Security officials from both sides confirmed casualties and injuries resulting from the fighting. However, while both side claim being provoked, neither side disclosed exact figures for those killed or wounded, citing the need to maintain operational secrecy. Residents on both sides said the fighting, which began around 5:30 a.m., appeared to ease around lunchtime but continued as of the time this report was compiled. Fighting spreads to other districts Residents and officials confirmed that the clashes spread to the East Borana Zone in the afternoon, intensifying in Melka Guba kebele in Gumi Eldallo District, Melka Adi and Melka Chophi kebeles in Wachile District, and Ela Orbi in Arero District. Transport movement in Moyale has come to a complete halt amid the fighting. Dozens of civilians, particularly women and children, have fled the town, while eyewitnesses and residents from both sides reported that numerous houses had been burned. Eyewitnesses who spoke to Addis Standard also said that, as of the time this report was compiled, neither the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) nor the Federal Police had intervened in the ongoing conflict. The latest fighting follows days of escalating tensions in Moyale after 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa was killed in an exchange of gunfire on 18 October, amid a dispute over the opening of a new Somali Regional State administration office and the raising of its flag. The dispute has since escalated into wider violence, with residents reporting casualties, property destruction, and displacement. Moyale, a flashpoint town administratively shared by Oromia and Somali regions, where areas under the two regional administrations are separated in places by a single lane, has repeatedly experienced clashes linked to territorial disputes between Borana communities in Oromia and Garre communities in the Somali Region. The clashes have resulted in deaths, displacement, and the burning of residents' homes. The conflict began on October 18, following the killing of a 13-year-old girl, which heightened tensions between security forces from the Oromia and Somali regions. Clashes erupted early on October 22, with reports of heavy gunfire and significant property damage, including the burning of homes. Residents have fled the area, and transport services have been disrupted. Both sides accuse each other of provocation, with claims of attacks and retaliatory violence. Eyewitnesses noted that the Ethiopian National Defense Force and Federal Police have not intervened. The ongoing violence reflects deeper territorial disputes between the Borana and Garre communities, exacerbated by administrative changes in the Somali Region that have previously led to significant unrest and displacement. The situation remains volatile, with casualties reported but unverified.

ethiopia.title: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Somalia: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: Peace Over Rivalry - Somalia's Future Lies in Cooperation, Not Confrontation With Ethiopia 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Somalia needs a foreign policy that gives its people a better chance of living in peace. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should place cooperation with Ethiopia at the center of that effort while protecting Somalia's sovereignty and maintaining its wider international partnerships. With so much unfinished work at home, Mogadishu cannot afford to let other governments' rivalries determine its relationship with its largest neighbor. The stakes are felt most clearly along a shared border stretching more than 1,500 kilometers. For pastoral families, traders, and communities connected by kinship, relations between the two countries are part of everyday life. A diplomatic rupture can mean a closed market, a disrupted journey, or greater insecurity. Those consequences deserve more weight in foreign policy than the visibility of a regional summit. Somalia has every right to build relations with Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and other partners. But each partnership should be judged by what it contributes to Somali security and recovery. Where another government's interests diverge from Somalia's, President Hassan Sheikh must preserve the freedom to choose his country's own course. Closer regional alignment becomes a liability if it draws Mogadishu into disputes with Addis Ababa that it has little ability to resolve or control. Moving beyond historical mistrust Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines This argument requires an honest account of history. Somali mistrust of Ethiopia did not emerge without reason. Under the EPRDF/TPLF-led government, military intervention and influence over Somali political actors left deep resentment. The 2006 intervention, when Ethiopian forces supported the Transitional Federal Government against the Islamic Courts Union, remains a powerful part of that memory. Cooperation will be difficult to sustain if those experiences are dismissed. As a former member of Ethiopia's House of Peoples' Representatives, I believe the region's leaders must take historical grievances seriously without allowing them to decide every future relationship. Communities on both sides of the border need governments willing to acknowledge past harm and negotiate a more dependable partnership. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's arrival in office in 2018 opened the way for a more constructive relationship with Somalia. Although Ethiopian troops continued operating in the country, the change in leadership offered an opportunity to move beyond the political interference associated with the previous administration. The task now is to consolidate that progress through security cooperation agreed with Somali authorities, respect for Somali institutions, and consistent restraint in Somalia's domestic political affairs. Mogadishu cannot afford to let other governments' rivalries determine its relationship with its largest neighbor." That responsibility is reciprocal. Ethiopia must respect Somalia's sovereignty, including in any negotiations over maritime access. Somalia should ensure that its territory and foreign partnerships do not support efforts to destabilize Ethiopia. Both governments have a legitimate interest in their neighbor's security, but neither should seek to determine the other's political future. Somali leadership, shared security The place of Ethiopian Somalis in national leadership also deserves attention. Ahmed Shide's election as Speaker of the House of Peoples' Representatives , Adem Farah's responsibilities as Vice President of the Prosperity Party and a federal official with Deputy Prime Minister rank, and Sultan Wolle's appointment as Minister of Irrigation and Lowlands place Somali leaders in positions of substantial national responsibility. In my view, these appointments reflect confidence in Somali leaders' contribution to Ethiopia's public life. Their importance is especially clear against a history in which the Somali region of Ethiopia was too often viewed through the concerns of security agencies. Representation is a right of citizenship, and its value must ultimately be measured by accountability and improvements in people's lives. Even so, the presence of Somali leaders in senior institutions is a meaningful part of contemporary Ethiopia that should inform a balanced assessment in Mogadishu. The two countries also share a security challenge that political disagreement cannot remove. Ethiopian forces formally joined the African Union Mission in Somalia in 2014 and have contributed to operations against al-Shabaab. Somalia has acknowledged the sacrifices of Ethiopian soldiers serving within African Union missions. That contribution merits recognition, alongside an insistence that all security arrangements respect Somali authority. The practical question is how to protect cooperation while Somalia strengthens its own institutions and assumes greater responsibility for national security. Mutual suspicion makes that task harder. When neighboring governments lose trust, armed groups gain room to exploit gaps in coordination. Neither country benefits from a relationship that leaves border communities more exposed. Case for practical cooperation President Hassan Sheikh could draw a useful lesson from President Ismail Omar Guelleh's engagement with Ethiopia. Djibouti has given its relationship with Addis Abeba a durable economic foundation through ports, transport corridors, and trade. These interests create reasons to keep talking when politics become difficult. Somalia can pursue a similarly practical approach, shaped by its own circumstances and priorities. The Ankara Declaration provides a basis for negotiated Ethiopian commercial access to the sea under Somalia's sovereign authority. Such arrangements would require clear terms, transparency, and safeguards for Somalia's long-term interests. Ethiopia, in turn, must pursue access through consent. If those conditions are met, port services and transport links could bring revenue and employment to Somalia while serving Ethiopian commerce. A functioning corridor can connect producers to markets and give businesses a reason to invest. Building those connections would give both governments something valuable to protect when disagreements arise. Prime Minister Abiy should strengthen that confidence through respect for Somali sovereignty and consistent restraint in Somali domestic affairs. We are concerned that, given the diversity of actors involved, these terms could be understood as a broad characterization of the armed opposition generally. We would therefore welcome further clarification of the context and intended scope of these references to help ensure that public interpretations accurately reflect distinctions among various movements, their stated objectives, and their conduct. We recognize the United States’ legitimate interest in regional stability and threats to civilian security. Although your remarks did not name any group, the principal armed opposition forces are widely known, and many belong to the newly formed Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political forces from all parts of the country. The Alliance has publicly stated that its objectives are to prevent national fragmentation, restore peace and stability, and enable Ethiopians to determine their country’s future through an inclusive political transition and democratic process. These stated objectives merit careful consideration in assessing whether the term “separatist” accurately describes the coalition. We do not ask the United States to endorse any armed or political organization or to accept its claims without scrutiny. Rather, we respectfully urge that assessments distinguish among an organization’s declared political objectives, independently verified conduct, and responsibility for specific incidents. Labels that do not account for historical and political realities behind Ethiopia’s present crisis risk obscuring the legitimate struggle of many Ethiopians for security, survival, dignity, and protection from gross human rights violations. Opposition to a government is not, by itself, separatism or terrorism; nor can political grievance justify attacks on civilians. The Alliance maintains that it resorted to armed struggle only after the space for peaceful political participation had effectively closed, and security conditions for many of its constituent communities had deteriorated sharply. It states its purpose as protecting the population and pursuing political change, not targeting civilians or employing terrorist tactics, a commitment it has demonstrated thus far in its conduct, including its military operations. Mr. Secretary, We do not exempt any armed actor from its obligations under international humanitarian law, and we support impartial accountability for unlawful attacks on civilians by all parties. That principle must apply equally to the regime in Ethiopia. The US State Department’s own 2024 Human Rights Report documented credible reports of unlawful killings, enforced disappearances, torture, and arbitrary detention by government security forces, with few, if any, officials held to account. Respected international and human rights organizations have further accused the Ethiopian military of war crimes, crimes against humanity, ethnic cleansing, conflict-related sexual violence, the weaponization of food, and genocide. Meanwhile, civilians in Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, and Benishangul-Gumuz continue to suffer aerial bombardment and artillery attacks. We urge the United States to condemn these abuses clearly and publicly, and to back that condemnation with concrete action, including support for independent investigations and targeted measures against those responsible. We also ask the Department to acknowledge the Alliance’s publicly stated commitment to Ethiopia’s sovereignty, unity, democratic transition, and national reconciliation, and to weigh those objectives alongside its verified conduct, as the United States supports efforts to promote peace and stability in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa subregion as a whole. Carefully calibrated language and balanced action strengthen U.S. diplomacy by reducing misunderstanding, discouraging escalation, and preserving space for inclusive dialogue. In keeping with your call for de-escalation and dialogue, we urge continued American engagement to support humanitarian relief, credible accountability, and an Ethiopian-led political settlement. We remain committed to an Ethiopia united through justice, mutual respect, equality, and the democratic consent of its people. We respectfully express hope that continued U.S. engagement will advance these principles and help create conditions for a just and lasting peace. Thank you for your consideration. Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Coffee Sector Faces $453 Million Export Risk Under EU Deforestation Rules 22 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia could lose up to $453 million in coffee export revenue under the European Union's deforestation regulation, with compliance gaps threatening to exclude smallholder farmers from a market that accounts for around 30% of the country's coffee exports, according to an October 2026 briefing paper by ODI Global. The study, The case of EUDR in Ethiopia : How to secure climate, trade and development goals, and overcome risks of market exclusion, warns that difficulties in tracing coffee to individual farms, documenting land-use legality and collecting plot-level geolocation data could expose up to 60% of smallholders to exclusion from EU-bound supply chains. The resulting disruption could reduce Ethiopia's gross domestic product by up to 0.5%, deepen foreign exchange shortages and transmit financial pressures through rural lending networks. The findings highlight a central challenge for Ethiopia as the EU prepares to enforce its Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): whether a policy designed to prevent forest loss can achieve its environmental objectives without imposing disproportionate costs on smallholder producers in developing countries. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Compliance gaps threaten smallholder access Ethiopia's coffee industry is particularly exposed because production is dominated by smallholders cultivating fragmented plots, many of which are less than one hectare. Around four million smallholder farmers account for approximately 95% of national coffee output, while the sector supports an estimated 15 million people across the value chain. The EUDR requires companies placing covered commodities on the EU market to demonstrate that products are deforestation-free and comply with relevant laws in their country of production. For coffee, this includes providing geolocation data linking shipments to the plots where the beans were grown. However, the ODI study identifies significant gaps in Ethiopia's preparedness. By July 2024, geolocation data had been compiled for approximately 200,000 hectares out of an estimated 860,000 hectares of coffee-growing land, equivalent to around 23%. Traceability presents another major obstacle. An estimated 57.4% of marketed coffee passes through local collectors or channels outside legally designated marketplaces, complicating efforts to track beans from individual farms through processing and export. The study estimates that geolocation constraints alone could put 10%-20% of smallholders at risk of exclusion, while traceability gaps could affect up to 57% of supply chains. Together with unresolved legal documentation requirements, these weaknesses could expose a substantially larger share of producers to exclusion. The consequences are already visible in parts of the sector. The Sidama Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union told researchers that it had excluded 40% of its member cooperatives from EU exports because of compliance constraints. Meanwhile, the Oromia Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union had collected geolocation data for only 92,000 of its more than 557,000 member farmers. Export losses could deepen economic pressures The potential losses extend beyond coffee-producing communities. According to ODI Global, Ethiopia could forfeit approximately $160 million in EU-destined coffee revenue under a scenario involving 20% exclusion, rising to $453 million if exclusion reaches 57%. These figures represent estimated gross export revenue losses, not necessarily the amount Ethiopia would ultimately lose after redirecting coffee to other markets. The study estimates that even if all excluded coffee could be sold elsewhere, lower prices in alternative markets could leave Ethiopia with net revenue losses ranging from approximately $42 million to $118 million. This distinction matters because Ethiopia has been expanding its coffee exports beyond Europe. The study notes that Asia accounted for approximately half of the country's coffee exports, compared with 28% for Europe and 12% for the United States. Yet EU-bound coffee often commands higher prices, making alternative destinations an imperfect substitute. The broader economic exposure is significant. Coffee accounts for approximately 35% of Ethiopia's merchandise export earnings, meaning EU-bound coffee represents an important source of foreign currency. ODI estimates that disruption to these exports could reduce foreign exchange earnings by between 2.2% and 6.3%, potentially reaching 8.5% under a severe scenario involving traceability and geolocation failures. Such a shock would compound existing pressures on foreign exchange availability, inflation and import costs. The study also warns that financial risks could spread through exporters, processors, cooperatives and banks that depend on coffee sales to service loans and finance seasonal procurement. Cooperative Bank of Oromia is particularly exposed because approximately 20%-30% of its loan portfolio is linked to coffee export financing, according to the study. Environmental objectives and local realities The study questions whether excluding Ethiopian smallholders would necessarily advance the regulation's environmental objectives. While deforestation remains a concern in Ethiopia, the researchers argue that coffee has not been a major driver of recent forest loss. Citing European Forest Institute data, the paper notes that no more than 20 coffee plots were linked to post-2020 deforestation. Ethiopia's coffee production systems frequently incorporate shade trees and forest cover. Garden coffee accounts for approximately half of national production, while semi-forest and forest systems contribute around 35% and 10%, respectively. The researchers warn that excluding farmers from higher-value European supply chains could weaken incentives to maintain these systems. Producers unable to meet compliance requirements may redirect their coffee to less-regulated markets or turn to alternative cash crops that could create greater pressure for land conversion. The paper therefore argues that compliance measures should be accompanied by incentives that reward sustainable production, including price premiums, carbon credits and payments for ecosystem services. Market diversification offers only partial relief Ethiopia has previously sought additional time to prepare for the regulation. In October 2024, the government welcomed the European Council's decision to postpone implementation by one year , following concerns over the costs and feasibility of meeting the original deadline. Addis Standard reported in April 2025, citing The New York Times , that Ethiopian coffee growers were struggling to meet the regulation's traceability requirements. Dejene Dadi, head of the Oromia Coffee Farmers' Cooperative Union, said the process was costly and difficult without additional support. The ODI study indicates that these concerns remain unresolved despite government efforts to establish national traceability systems and expand farm-level data collection. The Ethiopian Coffee Traceability Management System is intended to track coffee from production plots through processing and export. However, the researchers say its effectiveness remains uncertain while data collection, land registration and integration across supply-chain actors remain incomplete. A report by ODI Global highlights that compliance challenges could exclude smallholder farmers, who produce about 95% of the country's coffee, from EU markets, which account for roughly 30% of Ethiopia's coffee exports. The study indicates that difficulties in tracing coffee to individual farms and collecting necessary geolocation data could put up to 60% of smallholders at risk of exclusion. This disruption could reduce Ethiopia's GDP by up to 0.5% and exacerbate foreign exchange shortages. The EUDR requires proof that coffee is deforestation-free, but Ethiopia's current traceability systems are inadequate. The report warns that excluding smallholders may not effectively address deforestation, as coffee production often incorporates sustainable practices. The Ethiopian government is urged to engage with EU authorities to clarify compliance requirements and support smallholders in meeting these challenges.

New projections by IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding accounting for 92 percent of the projected displacement. The warning comes as Somalia enters a rainy season forecast to bring above-normal rainfall amid strengthening El Niño conditions. “We are looking at the possibility of hundreds of thousands of people losing their homes in just a matter of weeks. Many of these families have already been displaced before and have very little left to fall back on,” said Manuel Marques Pereira, IOM Somalia Chief of Mission. “There is still time to reduce the impact, but that window is closing. We urgently need funding to help people protect their homes and livelihoods, reach safer ground where necessary, and avoid another cycle of displacement.” A Response Severely Underfunded Despite the growing threat, IOM has secured only about 14.4 percent of the required $16.62 million needed to prepare for and respond to El Niño-related flooding. The funding is intended to support more than 517,000 people in flood-prone communities across Somalia. The shortfall is already constraining efforts to establish safe relocation areas and provide essential shelter, clean water, sanitation, and healthcare. IOM is working with Somali authorities and local communities to strengthen early warning systems, identify safer evacuation routes, and prepare emergency assistance, but the agency says the funding gap is limiting its ability to act at the scale required. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of national flood preparedness , the Somali Disaster Management Agency has placed 29 districts across 14 regions on high alert for riverine and flash flooding. The IOM’s warning confirms that the humanitarian system is not yet resourced to match that level of alert. Signs of Flooding Already Emerging Flooding has already begun in several areas. In Dollow, the Jubba River approached flood levels before receding, while the Shabelle River is rising toward the top of its banks in Jowhar. Heavy rainfall in Baidoa has already damaged homes and forced families to flee several neighborhoods. Beletweyne and Gaalkacyo are among the areas facing the greatest threat, with approximately 229,000 and 82,000 people respectively at risk of displacement. Families living in overcrowded displacement sites are particularly vulnerable, with assessments identifying inadequate access to safe water and sanitation, raising concerns about disease outbreaks if flooding intensifies. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Shabelle River , water levels at Jowhar rose by nearly a meter in 48 hours in mid-October, surpassing the high flood risk threshold and approaching bankfull. The FAO’s SWALIM advisory warned that flooding through open river breakages between Jowhar and Balcad was likely to continue and spread into nearby farms and villages. Beyond the Immediate Threat Rising floodwaters could destroy crops, disrupt livelihoods, contaminate water sources, and cut off access to healthcare and other essential services, deepening humanitarian needs in communities already affected by successive climate shocks. The displacement projections represent a cumulative estimate for the quarter rather than an even distribution over time. Similar to the 2023 El Niño floods, displacement is expected to peak during the height of flooding and gradually decline as conditions improve. The warning follows a pattern of repeated climate emergencies in Somalia. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the 2023 flood victims , communities devastated by the previous El Niño event are once again bracing for a repeat, with depleted coping mechanisms and little external support. Critical Note The IOM’s warning is precise, evidence-based, and urgent. The agency has done what it can: projected the displacement, identified the at-risk populations, mapped the river levels, and called for funding. What it has not done, and cannot do alone, is close the gap between the resources it has and the resources it needs. The 14.4 percent funding figure is the central fact of this crisis. It means that for every ten families at risk, the humanitarian system can currently reach fewer than one and a half. The early warning systems IOM is strengthening are necessary, but they are not shelter. The evacuation routes it is mapping are necessary, but they are not clean water. The emergency assistance it is preparing is necessary, but it is not funded at a scale that matches the projected need. The international community has repeatedly pledged to act on early warnings in Somalia. The 2023 floods demonstrated what happens when it does not. The current El Niño season is forecast to bring rainfall that could rival or exceed that event. The IOM’s warning is a test of whether the lessons of 2023 were learned, or whether they were noted, filed, and forgotten. The window to act, as Pereira said, is closing. The question is whether anyone with the resources to act is listening. On Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, issued a joint communique in Beijing expressing “serious concern” over threats to Red Sea shipping and calling for the Horn of Africa to be kept free from geopolitical rivalry. The statement warned that recent tensions pose a “serious threat to the global economy, particularly to economic activities in the Horn of Africa region, including trade, investment, energy, and food security.” The communique placed the onus for resolving the crisis on the broader Middle East conflict, stating that “easing tensions in the Middle East is key to resolving the security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.” It called on “all parties” to take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy, but offered no specific new mechanisms or commitments from either China or Djibouti to facilitate that process. Washington’s Parallel Initiative On the same day, the U.S. Embassy in Djibouti announced a different kind of engagement. Ambassador Cynthia Kierscht joined the Djiboutian Coast Guard and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) to inaugurate the Maritime Rule of Law Center of Excellence at the Doraleh Coast Guard Training Center. Funded by the United States, the center is described as a regional training hub designed to strengthen the capabilities of maritime law enforcement forces throughout the Western Indian Ocean. The embassy statement framed the initiative as a contribution to “defending American interests in security and the economy by protecting essential maritime routes, securing American trade, and promoting safe and secure international commercial exchanges.” A Crowded Military Landscape Djibouti’s strategic value is perhaps best illustrated by the extraordinary concentration of foreign military power on its soil. The small nation hosts bases from several major powers, often located within a few miles of one another, turning the country into a dense hub of global military infrastructure. The most prominent presence is the United States, which operates Camp Lemonnier, its largest permanent military base in Africa. Home to over 4,000 personnel and the Combined Joint Task Force-Horn of Africa, it serves as a platform for counterterrorism and crisis response operations across the region. Just miles away sits China’s only formally acknowledged overseas military base, established in 2017. Initially a logistics hub for anti-piracy patrols, it has been significantly upgraded with advanced communications and signals intelligence facilities, giving Beijing a persistent forward node for monitoring the region. France maintains its largest overseas base outside of its territory, with roughly 1,500 personnel and permanent maritime, air, and land capabilities. Japan operates its only overseas Self-Defense Force facility, focused primarily on counter-piracy and regional information gathering. Italy also maintains a base, while Russia has reportedly sought access for naval logistics and resupply, though it does not have a permanent base there. Djibouti, for its part, is positioned as the indispensable partner for all of them. Its geography, straddling the Bab el-Mandeb, gives it leverage that few other states possess. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Djibouti’s regional diplomacy , President Ismail Omar Guelleh has cultivated relationships with China, the United States, France, Türkiye, and Gulf states simultaneously, a balancing act that has allowed the small nation to extract resources and security guarantees from multiple suitors while warning against unilateral actions that threaten regional stability. The Deteriorating Security Environment The context for both initiatives is a rapidly deteriorating security environment. The UN Special Envoy for Yemen warned in October that the country has “slid back into full-scale war,” with Houthi forces advancing on Mokha and the Bab el-Mandeb coast before a government counter-offensive retook some areas. Houthi attacks on shipping have continued, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations reported explosions near a vessel off Mocha in early October, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Red Sea shipping threats . China’s approach, as reflected in the communique, is diplomatic and declaratory. It expresses concern, calls for dialogue, and positions Beijing as a neutral voice advocating for regional stability without committing new resources or taking operational responsibility for maritime security. China’s direct stakes are substantial: the Red Sea is a vital link for Chinese exports to Europe, and Beijing has invested over $5 billion in Egypt’s Suez Canal Economic Zone and significant sums in Djibouti’s ports and the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway. The U.S. approach is operational and capacity-focused. The Maritime Rule of Law Center is a tangible investment in the institutions that enforce maritime security on the water. It builds on Camp Lemonnier and partners with UNODC to provide training that directly addresses the operational gaps that allow piracy, smuggling, and maritime crime to flourish. What This Means for Somalia For Somalia, the intensifying competition between China and the United States in Djibouti is not a distant geopolitical spectacle. It is a development that directly affects the country’s economic and security trajectory. The Red Sea crisis has already driven up fuel and food prices in Somali markets, disrupted shipping routes, and revived piracy in Somali waters as international naval assets pivot toward the northern Red Sea. The new U.S. training center in Doraleh will strengthen maritime law enforcement capabilities in the Western Indian Ocean, but its primary beneficiaries will be Djibouti and the broader regional architecture that Washington is building to secure its own trade interests. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the U.S.-Djibouti naval training , this collaboration reinforces the security architecture of the Bab el-Mandeb at its narrowest point, while the Somali coastline that opens onto the same corridor remains largely unguarded. Somalia’s coast guard and navy remain under-equipped and under-resourced, and the country’s coastline, the longest in mainland Africa, continues to be a zone of illegal fishing, arms smuggling, and pirate activity. The asymmetry is stark. Djibouti hosts the largest permanent U.S. military base in Africa and has received sustained international investment in its navy, including patrol boats, radar surveillance systems, and training programmes. Somalia’s maritime-security apparatus operates primarily around Mogadishu, with limited reach beyond territorial waters, and remains reliant on sporadic international support. The two countries have sought to deepen their partnership in other areas. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Mogadishu-Djibouti port partnership , the directors of both ports have held strategic talks aimed at expanding cooperation, improving cargo management systems, and aligning infrastructure development to support faster, more efficient trade. The two nations have also strengthened defense ties through ministerial meetings, with Somalia’s Defense Minister expressing deep appreciation for Djibouti’s contributions to AUSSOM and regional stability, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the defense talks . But these partnerships do not close the maritime security gap. Djibouti’s capacity is being reinforced by the United States, the EU, and other partners. Somalia’s capacity remains nascent. Meanwhile, China’s diplomatic communique with Djibouti does not mention Somalia, nor does it offer any new commitments to address the piracy resurgence or the humanitarian impact of the shipping crisis on the Somali economy. The statement’s call for the Horn of Africa to be kept free from geopolitical rivalry is a sentiment Mogadishu shares. But Djibouti, not Somalia, is the venue where these two powers are choosing to coordinate their approach. Somalia is left to manage the fallout without the resources or the strategic attention that its geography and exposure would warrant. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the regional fallout , the U.S. State Department has already warned of potential escalation beyond the immediate zone of hostilities, with consequences for U.S. interests and institutions worldwide, including in Somalia. Critical Note The dueling Djibouti initiatives this week are a microcosm of how the two superpowers approach the Red Sea crisis. China issues communiques and calls for dialogue, positioning itself as a neutral advocate for stability while protecting its commercial interests. The United States funds training centers and builds operational capacity, reinforcing its role as the region’s security guarantor. Neither approach is sufficient on its own. China’s communique is correct in its diagnosis: the Red Sea crisis cannot be resolved without addressing the Middle East conflict that fuels it, and the Horn of Africa should not become a geopolitical battleground. But diagnosis is not a strategy. The communique offers no mechanism for de-escalation, no commitment of resources, and no accountability for the parties whose actions are destabilizing the waterway. The U.S. center is a practical investment, but it addresses the symptoms of maritime insecurity, not their causes. Training coast guards to intercept smugglers and pirates is valuable. It will not stop Houthi missiles or resolve the Yemen war that has made the Bab el-Mandeb a front line. For Somalia, the lesson is one of exposure without leverage. The country’s waters are part of the same security environment that Djibouti is being paid to help manage. But Somalia is not receiving the training center, the diplomatic communiques, or the strategic attention. It is absorbing the costs of a crisis it did not create and cannot control. Djibouti leverages its geography to extract rent and security guarantees from multiple global powers. Somalia, with the longest coastline in mainland Africa, lacks the naval capacity to protect its waters, the economic resilience to absorb sustained shipping disruptions, and the political cohesion to present a unified front on regional security. The competition between China and the United States in Djibouti is not a contest Somalia can influence. It is one whose consequences Somalia will bear. The new leadership comprises Speaker Abdiqani Lukman Haji Abdi, First Deputy Speaker Abdirahman Abdi Iidow, and Second Deputy Speaker Jama Ali Mohamud. They were elected during a parliamentary session in Jowhar, completing the formation of the legislative leadership ahead of the regional presidential vote scheduled for tomorrow, October 24. Federal Congratulations and Calls for Diligence President Mohamud extended his congratulations to the new leadership, commending them for the confidence placed in them by the lawmakers. He urged them to fulfill their constitutional duties with diligence and integrity, and to work toward strengthening governance, consolidating democracy, and accelerating the work of the regional parliament. The president also emphasized the importance of inter-institutional cooperation, social unity, and reinforcing peace and development in Hirshabelle. Speaker Nur, in a separate statement, similarly praised the new leadership and called on them to serve the people of Hirshabelle with transparency and accountability. He urged the new speaker and his deputies to focus on enhancing cooperation between government institutions, improving public representation, and prioritizing the general interests of the people of Hirshabelle and Somalia as a whole. The congratulatory messages from the federal leadership underscore the political significance of the Hirshabelle transition. The regional parliament was elected in a direct vote on September 30, with the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) securing 78 of the 99 seats, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the electoral timetable . That overwhelming majority means the JSP effectively controls the selection of the new speakership and, by extension, the upcoming presidential vote. The Road to the Presidency The election of the parliamentary leadership clears the way for the regional presidential vote on Saturday. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the schedule , candidates for the presidency and vice-presidency are expected to submit their applications on Friday, October 23, with speeches and the final vote taking place the following day. The JSP has nominated incumbent President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlaawe for another term, a decision that has sharpened a long-running power-sharing dispute between the Hawadle community of Hiiraan and the Abgaal community of Middle Shabelle. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Beledweyne protests , residents and traditional elders warned that they would not accept elections without a prior political agreement on the region’s leadership. Hirshabelle Vice President Yusuf Ahmed Hagar Dabageed, a Hawadle politician, has publicly accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of reneging on a promise to return the regional presidency to the Hawadle clan. The JSP has selected former Hiiraan governor Abdifatah Hassan Afrah as its vice-presidential candidate in an attempt to balance the ticket. Critical Note The congratulatory messages from President Mohamud and Speaker Nur are standard diplomatic and political courtesies, but they carry a particular weight in the Hirshabelle context. The regional parliament’s election was a significant step toward direct representation, replacing the indirect clan-based selection system that had governed the state since its formation. But the federal leadership’s praise for the new speakership cannot obscure the unresolved political tensions in the region. The JSP’s 78-seat majority in the regional assembly means that the new speaker and his deputies were elected by a chamber that the ruling party dominates. The Hawadle community’s demand for the presidency remains unaddressed, and the selection of a former Hiiraan governor as the JSP’s vice-presidential candidate has not resolved the underlying dispute over power-sharing. The new parliamentary leadership now faces the task of presiding over a presidential election that is expected to return Guudlaawe to office, but whose legitimacy is contested by significant constituencies in Hiiraan. A parliament elected directly is a step forward. A parliament that elects a president without addressing the grievances of its region’s second-largest community is a step that may produce a government but not the political trust that Hirshabelle has lacked since its formation. The federal congratulations are a starting point. They are not a resolution. Richard Giedroyc Published Oct 23, 2026 12:04 AM PDT Share this story Somalia hopes to issue new bank notes in the near future. The dollar bill is estimated to last about six years in circulation . Can you imagine what a bank note would look like if it had to last for 35 years? That is the predicament that has happened in Somalia. The nation, which stretches across the Horn of Africa, suffered through a civil war between 1991 and 2006. The insurgency that followed the establishment of the Transitional Federal Government of Somalia continued through 2012. The constant warfare left Somalia as being one of the least developed nations on earth. Currently, there is a Federal Government of Somalia, but insurgents continue to control parts of the beleaguered nation. Livestock and US currency function as money alongside 35-year-old Somali banknotes that are now increasingly being refused by merchants due to their ragged condition. So, why doesn’t Somalia simply arrange to have fresh banknotes printed? The transitional government revived the defunct Central Bank of Somalia during the late 2000s. A lack of confidence in the Somali shilling and the release of the few notes that were available inadvertently fueled inflation, and the dollarization of the economy followed. Somalia residents living abroad encouraged dollarization via sending U.S. currency home through money transfer networks. Adding to this confusion, Somaliland declared its independence and, since 1994, has been issuing its own shilling currency . Somaliland is not recognized internationally; however, the region continues to use its own coins and bank notes. Due to inflation, the 100-, 500-, 1,000-, and 5,000-shilin bank notes are the only denominations reported to be in circulation. These notes are dated through 2011. The breakaway government planned to issue notes in 2017 and 2022; however, none were able to be verified at the time this article was being written. As for Somalia, a 2017 International Monetary Fund report indicated a staggering 98% of Somalia bank notes in circulation were counterfeit . Transparency is a problem. Sources indicate bank notes in denominations of 1,000, 2,000, 10,000, 20,000, and 50,000 shillings were printed in Sudan. In 2022, former bank governor Abdisalan Omer Hadliye said bank notes were “lying idly” in a Sudanese warehouse, but the notes had been printed by an unnamed German company. There have been continual promises of a new currency, yet none has been reported to date. Through mid-2026, Somalia’s inflation was as high as 9.34%, partially influenced by the increased conflict going on in the Middle East involving Iran and the United States. Currently, Somalia’s parliament is considering a Currency Board Arrangement , finalizing bank reserve management, and regulations regarding foreign exchange. No announcement has been made regarding whether newly designed notes would be issued, and if so, who would print them. According to Somalia Commerce Minister Gamal (Jamal) Mohamed Hassan, “There is a process underway to get new banknotes,” continuing that the central bank has made “issuing a viable national currency and strengthening monetary policy tools” a priority. The Somalia government and central bank are under immense pressure to get a form of domestic currency into circulation. In 2027, the United States will cease supporting United Nations logistical backing for the nearly 12,000-strong African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia. This will impact the nation’s ability to obtain food, fuel, medical services, and troop transport. In addition, an estimated 1,100 Somalis living in the United States, many of whom have been sending dollars home via electronic systems, may be deported in the near future. On September 2, Central Bank Governor Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi said, “We cannot have a monetary policy without reintroducing the Somali shilling…issuing a viable national currency and strengthening monetary policy tools is a strategic priority.” Numismatics from Around the World: Around the World: Complementary Currencies Popular Around the World: No Future Harriet Tubman Note Around the World: AI Creates Fake Cambodia Bank Notes Share this story around the world Central Bank of Somalia Somalia currency Richard Giedroyc Author Related Stories Paper Money Auction: A “Most-Wanted” Note at Heritage Bank Note Reporter Staff Collecting 101 The History of Hawaiian Currency-Part 1 Rick Melamed Paper Money The First National Bank of Davenport, Iowa Fred Glueckstein US Coins Historic 1792 Half Disme Sets $2.93 Million Record, Leads Heritage’s $19 Million-Plus GACC Auctions Heritage Auctions Collecting 101 Around the World: Complementary Currencies Popular Richard Giedroyc Paper Money Notes from Washington: Serial Number Ranges for $2 1928 Red Seals Peter Huntoon © 2025 Active Interest Media All rights reserved. (AFP) MOGADISHU: Forces loyal to an ousted regional leader captured several key towns in southern Somalia, officials and eyewitnesses said Saturday, dealing a significant blow to the federally-backed local government. Several states in the deeply fragmented country are opposed to control by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, and in March his government sent in troops to oust the head of South West State, Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. advertisements Since then Laftagareen has repeatedly attempted to retake the region and its main city of Baidoa. On Saturday, military officials said his forces had taken the towns of Berdale, Dinsoor, Buurhakaba, and Qansaxdheere, as well as Awdiinle town — roughly 30 kilometers (18 miles) from Baidoa — leaving the local government and allies without control of the majority of the state. “The districts currently held by Laftagareen’s forces will be brought back under government control,” South West Information Minister Nur Sidow Baba told a press conference in Baidoa. Meanwhile, in a statement, Laftagareen commended the forces loyal to him on having “successfully recaptured and liberated four districts.” The rapid changes in control — while mostly conflict-free, although clashes were reported during the takeover of Buurhakaba — have left residents worried. “In Berdale, Darawish forces loyal to Laftagareen arrived on motorcycles, heavily armed, and took control without resistance,” resident Suleyman Nurow said. He said local officials fled to a nearby base hosting the African Union mission (AUSSOM) fighting Islamist group Al-Shabab, adding that Ethiopian troops remained inside and did not intervene. “We are confused by what is happening,” Dinsoor resident Adow Yusuf said, noting that forces allied to Laftagareen appeared to now be concentrating their efforts on towns surrounding Baidoa. “They have seized several districts in a short time, encountering resistance in only one,” he added. The victory sends Somalia into Monday’s final against Uganda, which had already secured its place in the championship match. Somalia, the 2022 CECAFA U-17 champions, will be seeking another regional title. advertisements After a goalless first half, Rwanda took the lead when substitute Patrick Ujeneza dribbled past two Somali defenders before beating goalkeeper Khalid Nor. Somalia responded four minutes later through Mohamud Osman, who scored after Rwanda’s defenders failed to clear the ball. With the score level at 1-1 at the end of regulation time, the match went to a penalty shootout, where Somalia prevailed 5-4. “I am so happy that my players remained focused and came from behind to score and later win in penalties,” Somalia coach Dadir Ami Ali said. “We now go and prepare for the final against a strong Uganda team.” The result continues Somalia’s campaign in the regional qualifying tournament for the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations. Somalia’s Minister of Youth and Sports, Mohamed Abdukadir Ali, and Somali Football Federation President Ali Abdi Mohamed Shiine, who also serves as vice president of CECAFA, congratulated the players and coaching staff following the victory. The officials praised the team's performance and determination in reaching the final. Somalia previously won the CECAFA U-17 Championship in 2022 and will have an opportunity to claim another title when it faces Uganda on Oct. 19. Meanwhile, Rwanda will face Ethiopia in a third-place playoff on the same day, with the winner securing the region’s third qualifying berth for the 2027 CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations. The map, shown during Netanyahu’s Oct. 18 presentation on regional security threats and alliances, depicted Somaliland and Puntland separately from the rest of Somalia and placed them in a category of territories considered friendly to Israel and the United Arab Emirates. advertisements “The Federal Government of Somalia strongly condemns and rejects the misleading map presented during the recent press briefing by the Prime Minister of the State of Israel, which depicts the Federal Republic of Somalia as fragmented and violates our internationally recognized borders,” Somalia’s Information Ministry said in a statement. The government reaffirmed that both Somaliland and Puntland are part of Somalia and rejected any foreign representation suggesting otherwise. “Somali territories, including Somaliland and Puntland, are integral and inseparable parts of the unified Somali nation,” the ministry said. Mogadishu described any effort by foreign governments or officials to redraw or misrepresent Somalia’s political map as a violation of international law and diplomatic norms, and called on international organizations and partner countries to respect its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The map was not created by the Israeli government. It matches a graphic published in May by Germany’s Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung examining competing geopolitical alignments in the Middle East and Horn of Africa. Netanyahu displayed the graphic while outlining what he described as emerging regional security blocs. Under the map’s color coding, Somaliland and Puntland were listed among territories considered friendly to Israel and the UAE. The rest of Somalia and the separately marked North East State were placed in another grouping associated with Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. The classifications represent the mapmakers’ assessment of regional alignments rather than formal alliance memberships. Somalia’s protest comes amid already strained relations with Israel over Somaliland. Israel formally recognized Somaliland in December 2025, a decision Somalia rejected as an infringement on its sovereignty. Mogadishu maintains that Somaliland, which declared independence in 1991, remains part of Somalia despite operating its own government, security forces and institutions for more than three decades. Puntland, by contrast, is a federal member state of Somalia and has not declared independence. The map’s depiction of Puntland in a separate geopolitical category therefore drew particular attention in Mogadishu. Somalia has repeatedly sought backing from the United Nations, African Union, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation for its territorial integrity following Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. The federal government said it remained committed to “safeguarding the sovereignty of its nation” and protecting Somalia’s unity. The dispute adds another diplomatic flashpoint to growing strategic competition around the Horn of Africa and Red Sea, where Türkiye, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and other regional powers have expanded their political, economic and security engagement in recent years.
